verdict.outcome: IT WORKS, IT IS EXACT, AND IT IS FASTER. First thing in this whole effort to beat the JAX path.

equivalence.reading: 1.788e-07 is f32 round-off, so the kernel computes the same function as the six-roll reference

what_unlocked_it.why: Every earlier attempt died on the same thing: no way to shift data inside a kernel. Mosaic GPU refused iota layouts, array slicing, ref slicing, concatenate and axis reductions. Pallas's Triton lowering refused non-power-of-two shapes and `slice`, which is what jnp.roll becomes. The masked indexed load is how a stencil is written in Triton in the first place, and it sidesteps all of it.
three_problems_it_removes: BlockSpec tiling: with memory_space=pl.ANY the ref stays in global memory and we do the addressing, so there is no block shape to make legal.
N = 39 not being a power of two: the index arrays carry a mask, so a 64x64 index grid simply overhangs and the masked lanes are discarded.
The three spin components: loaded one at a time with a scalar component index, which also removes the axis reduction the normalisation needed.
api_discovery: the backend is selected with compiler_params=pltriton.CompilerParams(), since the `backend` argument was removed in jax 0.9.1
load takes the ref ALONE: the index goes in ref.at[...], not as a positional argument
`other` requires `mask`; with pre-wrapped indices neither is needed for correctness beyond the overhang mask
what_unlocked_it.deprecation_note: the Triton backend was deprecated in jax 0.11.0 and this runs on 0.10.2, so the route has a shelf life

the_tile_is_fixed: T = 64 is a constant independent of B, and the grid is (B, Lz), so the work per program does not change with the batch size. That is the fixed-tile property the sawtooth argument needed. The measured times are still jagged, which is not yet explained and may be the rest of the program or noise.
limits: This is the STENCIL only -- the neighbour sum plus the normalisation -- not the full Metropolis step. But the stencil is exactly what the six rolls do, which is the 31.5% of runtime we were aiming at.
Four batch sizes, nine repeats, ONE run. The win is not uniform: +5.4% at B=96.

Absolute times are not comparable with earlier runs: the JAX reference measured 0.355/0.323/0.250 ms here against 0.206/0.176/0.171 ms in the Mosaic GPU run, so that container was in a different state. Only the within-run ratio means anything.
To deploy it the Metropolis physics would still have to be ported into the kernel, or the stencil result fed back into the existing JAX code, which would reintroduce a materialisation.
